questions.objective: Explain the purpose and scope of the Model Context Protocol and the integration problem it standardizes
questions.prompt: A platform team wants one model to read from a ticketing system, a code repository, and a wiki, and previously built a separate custom integration for each pairing of application and model. What problem does MCP standardize away?
options: The cost of paying for a separate model subscription for each connected application
The N times M growth of custom integrations, now replaced by a single shared protocol
The need for the ticketing system and the wiki to run on identical hardware
The requirement that a security team review every tool call before it reaches a server
questions.explanation: MCP replaces the combinatorial growth of custom point to point integrations with a single shared protocol, so any compliant application and any compliant model can interoperate without a bespoke connector for every pairing.

questions.objective: Describe the core MCP concepts and the roles of hosts, clients, servers, and tools
questions.prompt: In MCP terminology, which single statement correctly matches a role to its responsibility within one running session?
options: A tool is the separate program that exposes capabilities over a single active connection
A server is the user facing application that a person opens and directly types into
A host is the application the user runs, and it embeds one or more clients
A client is the reusable action a model decides to invoke during a conversation
questions.explanation: Each MCP role has one responsibility. The host is the user facing application that embeds one or more clients, while the client, server, and tool play distinct, separate roles within that same session.

questions.objective: Reason about the interoperability and value of one open protocol over per-system custom integrations
questions.prompt: A vendor argues that a single well documented open protocol is worth adopting even though each individual custom integration could theoretically be made to work. Which two reasons support that argument? Select two.
options: A custom integration is nearly always faster to build than adopting any shared protocol at first
A server built once against the protocol can be driven by any compliant host
A shared protocol guarantees that every connected system will always have identical performance characteristics too
Teams stop re-implementing the same authentication, discovery, and error handling logic for every pairing
questions.explanation: Interoperability value comes from writing integration logic once against a shared contract instead of per pairing, and from a server working with any compliant host, not from a faster first build or guaranteed equal performance.

questions.objective: Explain the purpose and scope of the Model Context Protocol and the integration problem it standardizes
questions.prompt: A company already has working point to point scripts connecting one internal model to two internal systems. What is the strongest reason to still adopt MCP for a third connection?
options: MCP requires replacing the two existing point to point scripts before any new work begins
MCP only becomes useful once a company has connected at least ten separate systems
Adopting MCP removes the need for any error handling in the new connection
Standardizing on one protocol now avoids writing and maintaining a fourth bespoke integration later
questions.explanation: The integration problem MCP standardizes away keeps recurring with every new pairing. Adopting a shared protocol now avoids repeating the same bespoke integration cost for a fourth connection and every one after it.

questions.objective: Describe the core MCP concepts and the roles of hosts, clients, servers, and tools
questions.prompt: During a live session, which pairing correctly describes the relationship between a client and a server?
options: One client holds exactly one connection to exactly one server for that session
One host embeds exactly one server and zero or more independent clients
One client holds connections to every server the host has ever used in the past
One server holds a connection to every client running on the user's machine
questions.explanation: Within one MCP session each client owns exactly one connection to exactly one server, which keeps the connection graph predictable, while a host may embed several clients each paired with its own separate server.

questions.objective: Read the schemas and structured data that define MCP messages, capabilities, and manifests
questions.prompt: A tool definition declares an inputSchema with a required array and an enum on one property. What do these two fields control?
options: The order in which the host renders the tool's name and description to the user
Which arguments must be present and which values a constrained property is allowed to hold
Which server process is allowed to register this particular tool at startup
How many times the tool may be called within a single conversation
questions.explanation: A tool's inputSchema uses required to name arguments that must be present and enum to restrict a property to a fixed set of allowed values, and both are checked before the handler ever executes.

questions.objective: Distinguish the responsibilities of MCP hosts, clients, and servers and how they are wired together
questions.prompt: A single host application has two clients open, each connected to a different server process. How are these components correctly wired together?
options: Both clients share one connection object so either can call the other's tools directly
The two server processes communicate directly with each other without going through the host
Each client owns exactly one connection to its own server, and the host coordinates both
One client proxies requests for the other client whenever its own server is busy
questions.explanation: Each client in a host owns exactly one connection to exactly one server, and the host is the component that coordinates multiple such client and server pairs running side by side in the same process.

questions.objective: Trace the model interaction flow from a user request through a client to a server and back
questions.prompt: A user request needs a tool result before the model can finish its answer. Which two statements correctly describe how that request flows through the system? Select two.
options: The server's result flows back through the same client before the model sees it
The model executes the tool's code locally instead of asking the server to run it
The server sends the request directly to the user interface, bypassing the client entirely
The host's client forwards the tool call to the server and waits for its response
questions.explanation: A tool call always passes from the client that owns the connection to its paired server, and the resulting response returns through that same client before the model incorporates it into its answer.

questions.objective: Read the schemas and structured data that define MCP messages, capabilities, and manifests
questions.prompt: A tool's inputSchema lists a property with an enum of three values, and the caller supplies a fourth value outside that list. What should happen to this call?
options: The call succeeds because enum only applies to optional properties, not this case
The call is queued until the server adds the fourth value to its enum
The call succeeds and the handler silently substitutes the closest matching enum value
The call fails schema validation before the tool's own handler code ever runs
questions.explanation: An enum restricts a property to a fixed set of allowed values, so any argument outside that list fails schema validation and the call is rejected before the tool's own handler code ever runs.

questions.objective: Distinguish the responsibilities of MCP hosts, clients, and servers and how they are wired together
questions.prompt: Two different host applications each connect their own client to the same server process over separate connections. What does this arrangement demonstrate about MCP architecture?
options: A server is host agnostic, so unmodified it can serve more than one client
A single client can be shared safely across two unrelated host applications at once
The two host applications must merge into one process before either can connect
The server must be rewritten separately for each host that wants to connect to it
questions.explanation: A server targets the shared specification rather than any single host, so the same unmodified server process can accept connections from separate clients owned by different host applications at the same time.

questions.objective: Apply the request, response, and notification interaction patterns and handle their results
questions.prompt: A client sends a JSON-RPC message with a non-null id to a server. Under the request, response, and notification pattern, what must happen next?
options: Nothing, because messages with a non-null id never require a reply from the server
The server must eventually send back exactly one response matching that same id
The client must resend the same message until the connection is closed
The server may send back zero, one, or several responses at its own discretion
questions.explanation: A JSON-RPC message with a non-null id is a request, and the protocol obligates the receiving server to eventually send back exactly one response carrying that same id so the caller can match them.

questions.objective: Handle protocol and tool errors, including malformed requests and failed executions
questions.prompt: A client sends a syntactically valid JSON-RPC request, but the method name does not match any capability the server exposes. Which error code applies?
options: -32603, because the tool's own handler code raised while it was executing
-32700, because the payload could not be parsed as valid JSON at all
-32601, because the request names a method or tool the server does not expose
-32602, because the supplied arguments failed the tool's declared input schema
questions.explanation: Method not found, coded negative thirty two thousand six hundred one, covers a syntactically valid request whose method or named tool does not match anything the server currently exposes, distinct from a parsing or schema failure.

questions.objective: Identify the protocol primitives such as tools, resources, prompts, sampling, and roots and how they are used
questions.prompt: A server wants the model itself to generate a piece of text mid task, using the host's own model access rather than the server's. Which primitive fits this need?
options: A root, which tells the server which directories or URIs it may operate within
A resource, which exposes addressable content that a user attaches to context
A prompt, which is a reusable message template a user must explicitly select first
Sampling, which lets a server ask the client to run a model completion for it
questions.explanation: Sampling is the primitive that lets a server ask the connected client to run a model completion using the host's own model access, rather than the server needing its own separate model integration.

questions.objective: Walk the tool invocation lifecycle from discovery through call to result
questions.prompt: A tool call passes through several checkpoints before a result reaches the model. Which two checkpoints belong to that lifecycle? Select two.
options: The host renders a marketing banner before the tool call is dispatched
The tool's arguments are validated against its declared schema before execution starts
The request is parsed as valid JSON before any further processing begins
The user's billing account is charged before the tool handler starts running
questions.explanation: A tool call passes through checkpoints including parsing the raw request as valid JSON and validating its arguments against the declared schema, both of which occur before the tool's handler code executes.

questions.objective: Apply the request, response, and notification interaction patterns and handle their results
questions.prompt: A server needs to tell a client that a background resource changed, without expecting any reply at all. Which interaction pattern fits, and why?
options: A notification, because it has no id and by definition never receives a reply
A handshake, because only the initial capability negotiation can announce new information
A response, because responses are the only message type sent without being asked
A request, because only a request can carry information about a state change
questions.explanation: A notification carries no id, so by definition the receiver never sends anything back, which makes it the correct pattern for announcing a state change like a resource update without expecting acknowledgement.

questions.objective: Handle protocol and tool errors, including malformed requests and failed executions
questions.prompt: A tool's handler code raises an unhandled exception while running, but the server catches it instead of crashing the whole process. Which error code should the response carry?
options: -32600, because the original request was not a well formed JSON-RPC request
-32603, because the tool's handler failed internally after the call was accepted
-32601, because the method the client asked for could not be located
-32700, because the raw request payload could not be parsed as valid JSON at all
questions.explanation: When a tool's own handler raises while executing and the server catches that failure rather than crashing, the response should carry the internal error code, which is reserved for exactly this situation.

questions.objective: Locate the trust boundaries between host, client, server, and the tools a server exposes
questions.prompt: A server returns a tool result, and that text is about to be added to the model's context. Where does the trust boundary the host must enforce actually sit?
options: Between two different clients inside one host, since one client cannot trust another client's server
Between the model and the person typing into the host, since only humans need review
Between the host's own code and the server, since a server's output is untrusted content
Between the network and the operating system, since MCP is a transport level concern
questions.explanation: The trust boundary that matters here sits between the host's own code and the separate server process, because anything a server returns is untrusted content until the host treats and handles it as such.

questions.objective: Apply permissions and consent so a user approves what a server may see and do
questions.prompt: A user approves a side-effecting tool once, during one specific call. Under MCP's consent model, what does that approval cover?
options: Every tool the same server exposes, for the remainder of the session
Every server the host has ever connected to, now and going forward
Every future call to any tool at all, once any single approval has ever been granted
That one named tool call, not the whole server or the rest of the session
questions.explanation: Consent under MCP is scoped narrowly to the one named tool call a user actually approved, not to the server that exposes it or to the rest of the ongoing session as a whole.

questions.objective: Design auditability and observability so protocol activity can be traced and reviewed
questions.prompt: A team wants protocol activity to be traceable and reviewable after the fact, not just watched live. Which two design choices support that goal? Select two.
options: Chaining each log entry's hash to the entry before it, so edits are detectable
Writing an append-only audit log that is never edited once an entry exists
Logging only failed tool calls, since successful calls carry no review value
Keeping logs only in memory so they disappear the moment the server restarts
questions.explanation: Auditability after the fact depends on records that cannot be silently rewritten, which an append-only log and a hash chain linking each entry to the one before it both provide independently of real-time monitoring.

questions.objective: Apply permissions and consent so a user approves what a server may see and do
questions.prompt: A tool is annotated as read-only, meaning it reports on the world without changing anything. How should a host typically treat calls to that tool?
options: As eligible for auto-approval, since it cannot change anything outside the conversation
As requiring a second server to independently confirm the same read
As requiring the same explicit per-call consent as any side-effecting tool
As forbidden entirely, since only side-effecting tools are allowed to run automatically
questions.explanation: A tool annotated as read-only reports on the world without changing anything outside the conversation, which is exactly the property that makes it a reasonable candidate for automatic approval without per-call consent.

questions.objective: Choose risk and safety controls against tool poisoning, injection, and over-broad access
questions.prompt: A malicious server author writes a tool description containing hidden instructions aimed at the model, rather than at the human reading a short label. What risk does this represent?
options: A rate limit violation, since the tool is being called more than its cap allows
Tool poisoning, a tool's own description text is used to inject hidden model instructions
A protocol version mismatch, since the client and server negotiated different versions
A schema validation failure, since inputSchema would reject the extra text automatically
questions.explanation: Tool poisoning occurs when a server author embeds instructions meant for the model inside a tool's own description text, exploiting the fact that the model reads that description as part of its context.

questions.objective: Select operational use cases where MCP connects agents to real systems
questions.prompt: A platform team wants a concrete, high value first use case for connecting an internal support agent to real systems. Which option best fits an operational use case?
options: Renaming the internal ticketing system so its API matches the model vendor's style
Running a benchmark that scores the model on general knowledge trivia questions
Letting the agent look up and update real tickets in the existing ticketing system
Publishing a research paper describing the protocol's message format in detail
questions.explanation: An operational use case connects an agent to a real system doing real work, such as letting it look up and update actual tickets, rather than a paper, a renaming exercise, or an unrelated benchmark.

questions.objective: Map the roles, responsibilities, and adoption patterns of teams deploying MCP
questions.prompt: As a company rolls out MCP servers internally, who typically owns writing and maintaining a given server's tool definitions?
options: The host application's own developers, regardless of which team built the server
The end user, who edits the server's source code before each individual session
The model vendor, who must approve every tool definition before it can run
The server author, a team that targets the shared specification rather than one host
questions.explanation: A server author is the team that builds and maintains a server's tool definitions, and they target the shared specification itself rather than any single host, which is what keeps the server portable.

questions.objective: Reason about ecosystem and portability across MCP clients, servers, gateways, and registries
questions.prompt: A capstone review checks whether a server can be swapped between two different host applications without any change to the server's own code. What does that check actually verify?
options: That portability holds, since an unmodified server can be driven by any compliant host
That both hosts share the exact same user interface layout and color scheme
That the model vendor has certified both hosts against the same benchmark suite
That the server's audit log was migrated along with the swap between hosts
questions.explanation: Portability means an unmodified server can be driven by any host that implements the client side of the same protocol version, so swapping hosts without touching the server's own code is what that property predicts.

questions.objective: Select operational use cases where MCP connects agents to real systems
questions.prompt: A team is deciding where MCP adds the most near term value across its internal tools. Which situation best matches a genuine operational use case rather than a novelty demo?
options: A static slide deck listing tool names without any server actually running
A recurring workflow where an agent regularly reads and writes real internal records
A one-time conference talk showing a tool call against a server with no real data
A single manual test call made once and never repeated by anyone
questions.explanation: A genuine operational use case is a recurring workflow where an agent regularly reads and writes real internal records, which carries ongoing value, unlike a one-time demo, a static list, or an unrepeated manual test.
